11500: Atualmente são conhecidos em torno de 28.000 espécies de peixes descritas no mundo, das quais aproximadamente 41% são espécies de águas doces. O ecossistema aquático apresenta uma área de amplos estudos, o conhecimento sobre a dieta alimentar desses animais, reflete não apenas na diversidade de alimento disponível no local, mas também na escolha do alimento mais apropriado às necessidades nutricionais dos peixes. Este trabalho tem como objetivo descrever a dieta alimentar do Corydoras aeneus no Córrego Russo, do município de Tangará da Serra - Mato Grosso. O volume dos itens encontrados nos estômagos, foi obtido pela compressão do material com uma lâmina de vidro sobre uma placa milimetrada até a altura de 1 mm. Os itens alimentares foram agrupados nas seguintes categorias: resto de inseto (himenópteros), ovo de peixe, resto vegetal (resto de folhas e algas), resto animal (vértebras de peixe), semente e escama (escama de peixe). A proporção dos recursos disponíveis no estômago a partir do método de frequência de ocorrência mostrou que resto de inseto foi o item com maior ocorrência totalizando (66,67%), seguido de ovo de peixe (19,05%), resto vegetal (19,05%), resto animal (14,28%), (4,76%) de semente e escama. Resto de inseto representou (55,11%) do volume, seguindo de ovo de peixe (25%), resto animal (11,33%), resto vegetal (7,48%), e (0,54%) de semente e escama. O índice de importância alimentar indicou que (82,22%) da dieta foi composta por resto de inseto. Conclui-se que a dieta alimentar do Corydoras aeneus é composta principalmente por elementos de origem alóctone, prevalecendo o hábito alimentar insetívoro.

As curvas foram obtidas por censo visual (Categoria III), seguindo o protocolo IFIM (Instream Flow Incremental Methology). Foram estabelecidas 19 seções transversais em um trecho de 150m, com o objetivo de amostrar todos os tipos de meso e microhabitats existentes. Em cada campanha foram realizadas observações subaquáticas diretas, por dois mergulhadores treinados. Ao avistar um peixe ou um cardume, registrava-se as informações de número de indivíduos, tipo de substrato e tipo de comportamento. A posição de cada peixe foi marcada com auxilio de pequenos chumbos numerados, para posteriores medições das variáveis hidráulicas. Ao todo foram realizadas 30 horas de mergulho. Com a matriz de uso do habitat, foi possível sobrepor com a matriz de disponibilidade de habitats (obtida por topografia e medições de estrutura do canal realizada em cada seção transversal) e assim determinar as curvas de aptidão de habitat para cada espécie, utilizando o programa RHYHABSIM. As curvas de aptidão para o tipo de substrato indicaram que B. ornaticeps está associada uma grande variedade de tipos de substrato. Para A. multispinis, as curvas indicaram preferência por rochas e pedras, enquanto para G. brasiliensis, foram rochas e areia. As espécies apresentaram diferenças claras quanto à aptidão de habitats, corroborando a hipótese investigada.

The inappropriate use of the coastal zone over the last century has culminated, among other aspects, in habitat loss and the depletion of fishery stocks, which has led to biodiversity loss in many areas of the globe. This scenario is even more worrying for elasmobranchs, primarily because of biological traits such as late maturation, slow growth and low reproductive rate. These characteristics, combined with excessive fishing effort and habitat degradation, have resulted in a rapid decline of many populations. Among these, one of the most threatened species is the sawfish, Pristis pristis, owing to economic interest mainly in the sale of its dorsal fin, liver and rostrum, which places the species among the most threatened elasmobranchs in the world. Of the interviewees, 50.6% showed knowledge of the species and only 12 (14.8%) reported reasons for its disappearance. According to the interviewees, destructive fishing practices using explosives and nets with very small mesh were the main causes of the disappearance of the sawfish in the study region. Fishers also pointed out that the construction of a dam (UHE Pedra do Cavalo in 1985) immediately upstream of the estuary (about 20 km) severely modified the salinity regime of the estuary, thereby creating a further stress for the maintenance of already exploited populations. The frequency distribution by CT class showed that the species' CT range ran from 280 to 534 mm for males and from 310 to 593 mm for females. For weight, the range ran from 124 to 816 g for males and from 184 to 1,272 g for females. The pattern usually observed for elasmobranchs shows that females reach greater size and weight than males. Males predominate in all CT classes up to 460 mm. In the classes above 460 mm, more females are seen, suggesting possible sexual segregation. Seasonal distribution was irregular, with more specimens occurring during summer/2009 and autumn/2008. Likewise, the smallest animals are present in the winter and spring seasons.

We surveyed Potamotrygonidae fishes from Amazonian aquatic habitats of Loreto (Peru) that face high fishing demand, are of notable economic importance, and are little studied. The objectives were to assess diversity, ecological and fishery aspects, and threats. Fieldwork was carried out in the Nanay, Itaya and Amazon rivers (July-October, 2013); the material of the MUSM Ichthyological Collection was reviewed; official statistical analyses (DIREPRO Loreto) on catches, provenance and trade were processed; and visits were made to related aquarium dealers in Iquitos. The aquatic habitats assessed were described limnologically; catches were made with local methods, obtaining samples fixed (10% formalin) and preserved (70% ethanol). Forty-two specimens (1138 cm, disc width) were examined, and seven species in three genera were identified: Potamotrygon, Plesiotrygon and Paratrygon, with the highest richness in the first and the second and the highest abundance in the first and the third, respectively. With the georeferenced data a distribution map was produced, adding three recently described species (two Heliotrygon, one Potamotrygon). The catch and trade data (DIREPRO) for 14 years (2000  2013) show overexploitation: more than 300 thousand specimens (12,000  52,000 per year; 22 thousand annual mean). Nominally, 101 forms are exploited, and the magnitude of the extraction shows overfishing of stingrays in Loreto, especially of Potamotrygon motoro and Paratrygon aiereba. Considering the information analysed, intensive extraction negatively affects the populations of Potamotrygonidae in Loreto. Adequate taxonomic criteria are needed for recording stingray species. Updating the information in Peru would support the conservation categorisation promoted by Colombia for P. motoro and P. aiereba (strongly threatened species) according to IUCN guidelines, and in agreement with other conservation and management criteria (CITES). In conclusion, further taxonomic studies and greater geographic coverage in Peru are urgent (possible existence of as yet undescribed forms); ecological aspects should be addressed and the conservation status of stingray populations assessed, sharing the results with specialists from neighbouring countries in order to adopt joint measures of control, management and sustainable use of these elasmobranch species.

The fish families observed in the diet were Ariidae, Engraulidae, Ophichtidae, Sciaenidae and Trichiuridae. Cephalopods were present as Loliginidae and crustaceans as Penaeidae and Sergestidae. Overall, Ctenosciaena gracilicirrhus, Paralonchurus brasiliensis and Lolliguncula brevis were the most important items. Ontogenetic differences were observed, with neonates and juveniles having crustaceans and cephalopods, respectively, with the second-highest %IRI. As for sex, no significant variations in diet were found. The hepatosomatic index showed a tendency to decrease with growth, suggesting consumption of energy reserves during development. There was high dietary overlap between males and females, and between neonates and juveniles, but this value was lower between the latter two categories. Diet diversity was low, mainly for males and juveniles. Neonates and juveniles of S. lewini are predominantly piscivorous, feeding secondarily on crustaceans and cephalopods.
